function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

{"content": "   489|## Chapter 8: The Diagnosis
   490|
   491|*When the foundation cracks*
   492|
   493|### The Symptoms Nobody Named
   494|
   495|Nancy noticed the fatigue first, in the spring—a tiredness that sleep didn't fix, that coffee couldn't touch, that settled into her bones like winter settling into the ground. She mentioned it to Bob in passing, the way people mention minor complaints they don't expect to amount to anything. "I'm just rundown," she said. "Too much going on with the kids, the book deadline, everything. I need a vacation, not a doctor." Bob believed her or wanted to believe her. They had both been tired for years—that was the baseline condition of parents, of people building lives. Fatigue was the weather of their existence, unremarkable as rain. But the fatigue persisted through summer, deepened into autumn. Nancy developed other symptoms she didn't mention. She didn't tell Bob because telling would make it real. Because she was afraid. Because some part of her already knew, in the way that bodies know things before minds are ready to acknowledge them. Then she noticed the lumps. "You're going to the doctor.” "I love you, but you're being stupid. Go to the doctor." They went.
   496|
   497|### The Waiting Room as Purgatory
   498|
   499|The office smelled of disinfectant and anxiety, a combination Bob would come to associate with the entire medical system. They sat in molded plastic chairs, surrounded by people with their own unnamed fears, waiting for the nurse to call Nancy's name. Bob tried to read a magazine—*Sports Illustrated*, month old—but the words would not assemble into meaning. He kept looking at Nancy, who sat with her hands folded in her lap, staring at a spot on the wall where the paint had begun to peel. She looked small, suddenly. Fragile in a way she had never looked before. "It's probably nothing," Bob said, because someone had to say it. "Probably," Nancy agreed, but she didn't look at him. The examination was routine, almost dismissive. The doctor—a man in his fifties with the confident manner of someone who had seen everything—asked questions, ordered blood work and imaging and a needle biopsy with the bored efficiency of a mechanic diagnosing a faulty transmission. They walked to the car in silence. The winter sun was too bright, the air too warm for the weight that had settled between them. Bob unlocked the car, opened Nancy's door, and as she passed him to get in, he caught her scent—her shampoo, her skin, the particular essence of her that he had known for more than two decades—and felt a spike of terror so pure it took his breath away. He pushed the thought away. It was nothing. It had to be nothing. They had too much left to do.
   500|
   501|### The Words That Changed Everything
   502|
   503|Bob would remember the exact geometry of that office for the rest of his life: the desk positioned to give the doctor authority, the chairs arranged to receive bad news, the window behind the desk that looked out on a parking lot where people were going about ordinary lives, unaware that everything was about to change. The doctor didn't waste time with preliminaries. Perhaps he had learned that kindness, in these moments, took the form of clarity rather than cushioning. "The results shows a malignant tumor" he said. "About 3 centimeters. I'm sorry." Sorry. The word hung in the air, meaningless. Sorry for what? For the words? For the reality they described. For the fact that life included such moments. Nancy made a sound—not quite a gasp, more like the air leaving a tire. She reached for Bob's hand and found it already there, waiting, squeezing with desperate strength. "Cancer?" she asked, and her voice was strange, distant, as if she were asking about someone else. "Yes. Breast cancer, with progression to 5 lymph nodes. There are treatment options, but I want to be honest with you—this is serious." Bob heard the words, understood their dictionary meanings, but couldn't assemble them into emotional reality. These were terms from medical dramas, from newspaper obituaries, from other people's tragedies. Not from his life. Not from Nancy.
   504|
   505|The meeting continued discussion of referrals, next steps, planning. Bob took notes with the mechanical efficiency that had served him in engineering meetings, recording information his brain could not yet process. Nancy asked questions with strange calm, as if discussing a renovation project rather than her own mortality. It was only when they reached the parking lot that reality broke through. Nancy collapsed against the car, making sounds that weren't words—keening, animal noises of grief and terror. Bob held her, shaking himself, both crying in the winter sunlight while strangers walked past on their way to lunch or shopping or the thousand ordinary errands that would continue while their world ended.
   506|
   507|### The First Night
   508|
   509|They didn't tell the children. Not yet. They were living on their own, just starting to find their way. They would need to be told, prepared, supported through what was coming, but not tonight. Tonight, Bob and Nancy needed to be alone with the knowledge, to begin the process of absorbing something that couldn't be absorbed. The children were finally told with reassurances that Mom was going to be fine. Everything was not fine. Everything would never be fine again.
   510|
   511|"I'm going to fight this," Nancy said finally. "I'm not giving up." I want to see the kids graduate from college.  "Of course," Bob said. "We'll fight. We'll do everything." But even as he spoke, he knew that fighting was a metaphor they used because the reality was unbearable. cancer wasn't an opponent you could defeat through willpower. The statistics were brutal, the prognosis not good. They would fight because not fighting was unthinkable, but the outcome was already written in the biology of aggressive malignancy.
   512|
   513|### The Machinery of Hope
   514|
   515|The oncology consultations began immediately. Dr. Chen was in his forties, with the brisk competence of someone who had learned to manage grief without being consumed by it. He laid out treatment options with clinical precision: chemotherapy to slow progression, radiation for symptom management, chemotherapy with a possibility of clinical trials that offered long-shot possibilities.
   516|
   517|"Advanced breast cancer is difficult to overcome," she said, not sugarcoating. "But every case is different. Some patients respond better than expected. We'll do everything we can." This was before genetic testing and advanced modern drugs that are available now, they were so close but just not ready. Everything they could we did, in retrospect it provided a few more years, worth it to Nancy but not a cure. The chemotherapy made Nancy violently ill nausea that no medication fully controlled, fatigue that deepened into exhaustion, hair that fell out in clumps. She bought a wig. The tumor markers remained stubbornly elevated. The scans showed continued progression into her bones. Bob threw himself into research, the way he approached engineering problems—reading medical literature, consulting specialists, searching for treatments that might offer hope beyond the standard protocols. He found clinical trials, experimental therapies, alternative approaches that ranged from plausible to quackery. Nancy indulged his research initially, but it didn’t yield any relief.  Then the lifetime financial cap on bob’s insurance maxed out, Nancy was stressed by this as they resorted to using retirement savings, but they kept trying, kept living.
   518|
   519|### The Treatment
   520|
   521|The next months were a blur of hospital visits, chemotherapy, and waiting. Waiting for test results. Waiting to see if the treatment was working. Waiting to see if our daughter would live. The chemotherapy of the time was brutal. It killed the cancer cells, yes, but it also killed everything else—her appetite, her energy, her hair, the playful spirit that had once filled our home with laughter. She grew thin and pale, her body a battlefield where war was waged between medicine and disease
   522|
   523|### The New Normal
   524|
   525|They developed routines for the new reality. Nancy's good days and bad days, mapped and managed like weather patterns. The children visiting when they could. Bob reduced his hours at work, delegating responsibilities he would have handled himself six months before. His supervisors were understanding—cancer was common enough that everyone knew someone who had been through this—but understanding didn't change the reality that his career was suffering, that opportunities were passing him by, that his professional trajectory was flattening while his personal life collapsed. He didn't care. Or rather, he cared, but the caring was buried beneath more urgent priorities. The work that had once consumed him now felt trivial, abstract, distant from the concrete reality of Nancy's diminishing body, the children's grief, the household tasks that multiplied as Nancy's capacity diminished.
   526|
   527|Nancy, despite everything, tried to maintain her life. She continued to work with her nephew (who was a quadriplegic). She kept driving herself to live, she lived to see both children graduate from college and was so proud. Then she achieved her goal she slowly but steadily declined until one day she said I am too tired to go on, take me to the hospital. And that day she passed.
   528|
   529|### The Physiology of Grief
   530|
   531|Bob became, gradually, an expert on dying. Not through study, but through the brutal education of experience over many months. He learned the physical vocabulary of Nancy's decline—the way pain migrated and intensified, the digestive failures that robbed her of nutrition, the edema that swelled her limbs, the jaundice that yellowed her skin as her liver failed. He learned to manage medications, to read the subtle signs that indicated crisis or recovery, to navigate the medical system that treated Nancy as a case while Bob struggled to protect her personhood. The marriage transformed. They were no longer partners in the sense they had been—equal contributors to a shared project. Bob was becoming caregiver, nurse, manager of decline. Nancy was becoming patient, dependent, recipient of care she had never wanted to need. They fought about this, sometimes. Nancy hated her dependency, lashed out at Bob for helping too much or not enough, for treating her like an invalid or for not understanding her limitations.    531|Bob became, gradually, an expert on dying. Not through study, but through the brutal education of experience over many months. Bob struggled to find the right balance, to offer support without taking autonomy, to protect without smothering. The love between them had changed shape, become something harder and more desperate than the easy companionship of their early years, but it was still love.    534|

   545|### The Empty House
   546|
   547|By late winter, the children had returned to their own lives. Bob was alone in the house. Truly alone for the first time in thirty years.    552|
   553|### The Year of Firsts
   554|
   555|The first birthday without her. The first Thanksgiving. The first Christmas, the first New Year, the first spring that brought flowers she had planted and wouldn't see bloom.    556|
   557|They ate in silence, the turkey dry, the conversation forced, the absence at the head of the table louder than any words. 
   558|
   559|### A New Rhythm
   560|
   561|By spring, Bob had developed routines that weren't Nancy's routines.
